clinicalPearls: Defined by new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks' gestation combined with proteinuria or evidence of maternal organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, neurological, haematological) or uteroplacental compromise

Proteinuria is no longer mandatory for diagnosis when hypertension is accompanied by features such as thrombocytopenia, raised transaminases, renal impairment, pulmonary oedema, or cerebral/visual symptoms
Warning symptoms include persistent severe headache, visual disturbance (flashing lights, blurring), right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, and rapid oedema of the face and hands
HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a severe variant that can occur with only modest blood pressure elevation
Definitive treatment is delivery of the placenta; timing balances gestational age against maternal and fetal risk
Magnesium sulfate is used for seizure prophylaxis in severe disease and to treat eclamptic seizures, not as an antihypertensive
Antihypertensive therapy aims to lower dangerously high blood pressure to reduce maternal stroke risk while preserving placental perfusion
Low-dose aspirin from early pregnancy reduces incidence in women at high risk (prior pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, renal disease, diabetes, multiple pregnancy, antiphospholipid syndrome)
reference.pathophysiology: Pre-eclampsia originates in abnormal placentation: inadequate remodelling of the maternal spiral arteries by trophoblast leads to a poorly perfused, ischaemic placenta. The ischaemic placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors (such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 and soluble endoglin) that antagonise vascular endothelial and placental growth factors, producing widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction. This causes vasospasm, increased vascular permeability, activation of coagulation, and multi-organ hypoperfusion, manifesting as hypertension, proteinuria, hepatic and cerebral involvement, and fetal growth restriction.
additionalDifferentials: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Serial blood pressure measurement and urine protein quantification (protein:creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection)
Full blood count for thrombocytopenia and evidence of haemolysis
Renal function including serum creatinine and urate
Angiogenic markers (sFlt-1/PlGF ratio) where available to aid risk stratification
Fetal assessment with ultrasound growth, amniotic fluid volume, and umbilical artery Doppler
redFlags: Severe hypertension unresponsive to treatment threatening maternal stroke
Neurological signs (severe headache, visual loss, hyperreflexia with clonus) heralding impending eclampsia
Right upper quadrant pain with abnormal liver enzymes suggesting HELLP or hepatic haematoma/rupture
Pulmonary oedema or oliguria indicating organ failure
Fetal growth restriction with abnormal Dopplers or non-reassuring fetal status
reference.prognosis: With timely surveillance, blood pressure control, seizure prophylaxis, and appropriately timed delivery most women recover fully postpartum, though there is an increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular and renal disease. Severe or early-onset disease carries higher maternal and perinatal morbidity, and recurrence in future pregnancies is common.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because proteinuria is absent despite organ dysfunction
Underestimating severity in HELLP syndrome where blood pressure may be only mildly raised
Over-aggressive blood pressure lowering compromising placental perfusion
Failing to continue monitoring postpartum, when eclampsia and severe hypertension can still occur
Treating magnesium sulfate as an antihypertensive rather than as seizure prophylaxis
management: Delivery of the placenta is the only definitive cure, with timing balancing gestational age against maternal and foetal risk
Blood-pressure control with antihypertensives such as labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa, and intravenous hydralazine or labetalol for acute severe hypertension
Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis in severe disease and for treating eclamptic seizures
Antenatal corticosteroids to promote foetal lung maturity when preterm delivery is anticipated
Intensive maternal surveillance of blood pressure, platelets and liver and renal function alongside foetal monitoring with growth scans and umbilical artery Doppler
Recognise and manage severe complications including HELLP syndrome, pulmonary oedema and eclampsia
Continued postpartum monitoring, with low-dose aspirin prophylaxis and cardiovascular-risk follow-up for future pregnancies
